nodes.title: The character-indexed Fourier transform on a finite abelian group
nodes.statement: For a finite abelian group G of order N and f : G → ℂ, fourier f : AddChar G ℂ → ℂ is fourier f χ = N⁻¹ ∑_{x∈G} f(x) · conj(χ(x)): probability counting measure on G, counting measure on the dual, and indexed by the dual group AddChar G ℂ itself, with no isomorphism G ≅ Ĝ chosen. This is the canonical form of the source's bi-character transform, which the source itself names as the canonical alternative.
hypotheses: G a finite abelian group, written additively, N = |G| > 0
f : G → ℂ
proofSteps: Define fourier f χ := N⁻¹ ∑_x f(x) conj(χ x); this is RCLike.wInner with the constant weight RCLike.cWeight and the character in the first, conjugated, slot.
Identify it with the coordinate of f in the character basis AddChar.complexBasis, using character orthogonality for the normalised measure.
Derive inversion f(x) = ∑_χ fourier f χ · χ(x) from the basis expansion.
Derive the transformation rules (translation, modulation, negation, conjugation, precomposition with an isomorphism or a surjection) directly from the defining sum.
Compare with Mathlib's ZMod.dft on ZMod N through the explicit isomorphism ZMod N ≅ AddChar (ZMod N) ℂ: fourier f (zmodAddEquiv r) = N⁻¹ · dft f r.
acceptance: fourier of a character χ is the indicator of χ: coefficient one at χ, not N.
Inversion reconstructs f exactly, with no stray factor of N.
On ZMod N the transform is N⁻¹ times Mathlib's dft, so neither normalisation silently replaces the other.

api.statement: fourier (f + g) = fourier f + fourier g.

api.name: fourier_smul
api.statement: fourier (c • f) = c • fourier f.

api.name: fourier_single
api.statement: fourier (Pi.single a c) χ = (card G)⁻¹ · c · star (χ a).

api.name: fourier_character
api.statement: fourier (fun x => ψ x) χ = if χ = ψ then 1 else 0.

api.name: fourier_inversion
api.statement: ∑ χ, fourier f χ · χ x = f x.

api.name: fourier_inversion_reindex
api.statement: For any equivalence e : ι ≃ AddChar G ℂ, ∑ i, fourier f (e i) · e i x = f x: inversion through an explicitly supplied indexing of the dual, never an identification of the dual with G.

api.name: fourier_injective
api.statement: fourier is injective.

api.name: fourier_eq_basis_repr
api.statement: fourier f χ = (AddChar.complexBasis G).repr f χ.

api.name: fourier_eq_wInner
api.statement: fourier f χ = RCLike.wInner RCLike.cWeight (fun x => χ x) f; the character sits in the first slot because the library inner product conjugates its first argument.

api.name: fourier_eq_haarIntegral
api.statement: fourier f χ is the integral of f · star χ against Tau Ceti's Haar probability measure TauCeti.haarProb on Multiplicative G (discrete topology): the one-dimensional case of the Peter–Weyl coefficients.

api.name: fourier_translate
api.statement: fourier (fun x => f (x − a)) χ = star (χ a) · fourier f χ.

api.name: fourier_modulate
api.statement: fourier (fun x => ψ x · f x) χ = fourier f (χ / ψ).

api.name: fourier_neg
api.statement: fourier (fun x => f (−x)) χ = fourier f χ⁻¹.

api.name: fourier_conj
api.statement: fourier (fun x => star (f x)) χ = star (fourier f χ⁻¹).

api.name: fourier_reflection
api.statement: fourier (fun x => star (f (−x))) χ = star (fourier f χ): the source's reflection identity.

api.name: fourier_equiv
api.statement: For e : G ≃+ H, fourier (f ∘ e) (χ ∘ e) = fourier f χ.

api.name: fourier_quotient
api.statement: For a surjective q : G →+ H, fourier (f ∘ q) (χ ∘ q) = fourier f χ.

api.name: fourier_quotient_zero
api.statement: For q : G →+ H and χ nontrivial on ker q, fourier (f ∘ q) χ = 0.

api.name: zmod_character_comparison
api.statement: AddChar.zmodAddEquiv r x = ZMod.stdAddChar (x · r), the explicit isomorphism the cyclic comparison runs through.

api.name: fourier_zmod
api.statement: On ZMod N, fourier f (AddChar.zmodAddEquiv r) = N⁻¹ · ZMod.dft f r.

nodes.title: Normalised convolution on a finite abelian group
nodes.statement: For f, g : G → ℂ on a finite abelian group G of order N, nconv f g x = N⁻¹ ∑_{y∈G} f(y) g(x − y): convolution with respect to the probability counting measure. It is N⁻¹ times Mathlib's discrete convolution addRingConvolution, a normalisation adapter and not a new convolution theory.
hypotheses: G a finite abelian group, N = |G| > 0
f, g : G → ℂ
proofSteps: Define nconv f g := N⁻¹ • DiscreteConvolution.addRingConvolution f g, with nconv_apply giving the explicit sum.

nodes.title: Parseval and Plancherel for the character-indexed transform
nodes.statement: For f, g : G → ℂ, N⁻¹ ∑_x f(x) conj(g(x)) = ∑_χ fourier f χ · conj(fourier g χ), and in particular N⁻¹ ∑_x |f(x)|² = ∑_χ |fourier f χ|²: the transform is an isometry from L²(G, probability measure) to ℓ²(Ĝ, counting measure).
hypotheses: G a finite abelian group
f, g : G → ℂ
proofSteps: Expand both sides in the character basis using fourier_inversion.
Use orthogonality of characters for the normalised measure: N⁻¹ ∑_x χ(x) conj(ψ(x)) = [χ = ψ].
Collect terms to obtain Parseval; take g = f for Plancherel.
acceptance: The measures differ on the two sides — probability on G, counting on Ĝ — and the identity is false with both normalised or both counting.
For f = ⇑χ both sides equal 1.
For f = 1_A, Plancherel gives ∑_χ |fourier 1_A χ|² = |A|/N, the density — the source's equation (1).

nodes.title: The transform takes normalised convolution to the product
nodes.statement: For f, g : G → ℂ and χ ∈ AddChar G ℂ, fourier (nconv f g) χ = fourier f χ · fourier g χ.
hypotheses: G a finite abelian group
f, g : G → ℂ
χ ∈ AddChar G ℂ
proofSteps: Expand fourier (nconv f g) χ = N⁻² ∑_x ∑_y f(y) g(x − y) conj(χ(x)).
Substitute x = y + z and use conj(χ(y + z)) = conj(χ(y)) conj(χ(z)).
The double sum factorises into (N⁻¹ ∑_y f(y) conj χ(y)) · (N⁻¹ ∑_z g(z) conj χ(z)).
acceptance: The identity holds with no constant exactly because both the convolution and the transform are taken against the probability measure; with unnormalised convolution a factor N appears.
For f = g = ⇑χ it gives 1 · 1 = 1 at χ.
It is the audit's named missing identity for AC.0.

nodes.title: Additive energy in Fourier terms
nodes.statement: For finsets A, B ⊆ G, E(A, B) = N³ ∑_χ |fourier 1_A χ|² · |fourier 1_B χ|², where E is Mathlib's additive energy Finset.addEnergy.
hypotheses: G a finite abelian group, N = |G|
A, B finite subsets of G
proofSteps: Write E(A, B) = ∑_x r(x)² with r(x) = #{(a, b) ∈ A × B : a + b = x} = Finset.addConvolution A B x.
By the indicator computation, nconv 1_A 1_B = N⁻¹ · r.
Apply Plancherel to nconv 1_A 1_B: N⁻¹ ∑_x |N⁻¹ r(x)|² = ∑_χ |fourier (nconv 1_A 1_B) χ|².
Apply the convolution identity to the right-hand side and multiply through by N³.
acceptance: For A = B = G both sides equal N³: E(G, G) counts all N³ solutions of a + b = a' + b', and fourier 1_G is the indicator of the trivial character.
For A = B = {0} both sides equal 1.
The factor N³ is forced by the normalisations; this is the check that pins it.

|1_A(x)|² = 1_A(x), so the right side is |A|/N.
acceptance: For A = G it gives 1: fourier 1_G is the indicator of the trivial character.
For A = ∅ both sides are 0.
For A a singleton it gives 1/N, while each of the N coefficients has modulus 1/N.

nodes.title: The trivial upper bound for additive energy
nodes.statement: For finite subsets A, B of an abelian group, E(A, B) ≤ |A|² |B| and E(A, B) ≤ |A| |B|², where E is Mathlib's Finset.addEnergy. The reviewed audit records these bounds as missing from the pinned Mathlib, which has only the lower bounds |A||B| ≤ E(A, B) and |A|²|B|² ≤ |A + B| E(A, B) and the equality E(G, B) = |G||B|².
hypotheses: A, B finite subsets of an additive commutative group (cancellation is what is used)
proofSteps: E(A, B) counts (a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂) ∈ A × B × A × B with a₁ + b₁ = a₂ + b₂ (addEnergy_eq_card_filter).
The map (a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂) ↦ (a₁, a₂, b₁) is injective on that set, since b₂ = a₁ + b₁ − a₂; so E(A, B) ≤ |A|² |B|.
Symmetrically (a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂) ↦ (a₁, b₁, b₂) gives E(A, B) ≤ |A| |B|².
acceptance: For A = G, E(G, B) = |G| |B|² (Mathlib's addEnergy_univ_left): the second bound is attained.
For A = B a subgroup, E(A, A) = |A|³: both bounds are attained.
Without cancellation the injectivity fails; the lemma is stated for groups.

sources.match: The source proves the Fourier form for A = B (equation (5), which fourier-energy converts into E(A, A) ≤ |A|³). The combinatorial bound for two sets is the elementary count in the proof steps; no source was needed for it.

nodes.title: Shannon entropy, conditional entropy and mutual information
nodes.statement: For a random variable X with values in a finite type, H[X] = Σ_x p_X(x) log(1/p_X(x)) (natural logarithm), computed from the distribution. H[X|Y] = Σ_y p_Y(y) H[X|Y=y], I[X : Y] = H[X] + H[Y] − H[X,Y], and I[X : Y|Z] = Σ_z p_Z(z) I[(X|Z=z) : (Y|Z=z)].
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.

Mathlib has only the binary entropy function; this node is the general carrier, built on Real.negMulLog and ProbabilityTheory.cond. The planned names follow the Lean formalization of this paper (teorth.github.io/pfr), which is not a pinned library.
proofSteps: Define measureEntropy μ = Σ_s negMulLog(μ{s}) for a measure on a finite type, entropy X μ = measureEntropy(μ.map X), and the conditional and mutual versions as displayed.
Jensen (concavity of negMulLog): H[X] ≤ log|S| with equality exactly for the uniform distribution (A.1); and max_x p_X(x) ≥ e^{−H[X]} (A.2).
Chain rule H[X,Y] = H[X|Y] + H[Y] (A.3), by expanding p_{X,Y} = p_Y·p_{X|Y}.

I[X : Y] ≥ 0 with equality iff X, Y are independent (Jensen), giving (A.4)–(A.5). Conditioning and summing gives submodularity H[X|Y,Z] ≤ H[X|Z] (A.6)–(A.7), and I[X : Y|Z] ≥ 0 with the formula (A.9).
Invariance of entropy under injective relabelling, and H[U_s] = log|s| for the uniform distribution on a finite set.
acceptance: The source recalls these facts in Appendix A and uses them throughout; none is specific to additive combinatorics.

nodes.title: Entropic Ruzsa distance
nodes.statement: For probability distributions μ, ν on a finite abelian group G, d[μ; ν] = H[X′ − Y′] − ½H[X′] − ½H[Y′], where X′ ∼ μ and Y′ ∼ ν are independent (1.1). For random variables d[X; Y] = d[p_X; p_Y] depends only on the two distributions. The conditional distance is d[X|Z; Y|W] = Σ_{z,w} p_Z(z)p_W(w) d[(X|Z=z); (Y|W=w)] (A.14).
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
X and Y need not be independent, or even defined on the same space.
proofSteps: Define rdist(μ, ν) from the distribution of p.1 − p.2 under μ ⊗ ν, and condRdist as displayed.
Symmetry: X′ − Y′ and Y′ − X′ have the same entropy. Nonnegativity and |H[X] − H[Y]| ≤ 2d[X; Y] follow from max(H[X], H[Y]) ≤ H[X − Y] for independent X, Y (A.10)–(A.12).
For independent X, Y on one space, d[X; Y] = H[X − Y] − ½H[X] − ½H[Y]; for independent copies, the conditional distance is H[X′ − Y′|Z′, W′] − ½H[X′|Z′] − ½H[Y′|W′] (A.15).
Translation invariance, and d[U_H; U_H] = 0 because U_H − U_H′ is again uniform on H.
acceptance: d[X; X] = 0 only when X is uniform on a coset of a subgroup (Lemma 2.2), and d[X; Y] = 0 can hold for different distributions (p. 4).

nodes.title: Entropic Ruzsa triangle inequality (A.13)
nodes.statement: For probability distributions on a finite abelian group, d[X; Y] ≤ d[X; Z] + d[Z; Y]; equivalently H[X − Y] ≤ H[X − Z] + H[Z − Y] − H[Z] for independent X, Y, Z.
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
proofSteps: Submodularity (A.6): H[Y − Z|X − Y] ≥ H[Y − Z|X − Y, Y] = H[Z|X, Y] = H[Z], using independence.
H[Y − Z|X − Y] = H[X − Z, Y − Z] − H[X − Y] ≤ H[X − Z] + H[Y − Z] − H[X − Y] by (A.5). Combine; the half-entropies in d cancel.

nodes.title: Madiman's inequality (Lemma A.1)
nodes.statement: For independent X, Y, Z in a finite abelian group, H[X + Y + Z] − H[X + Y] ≤ H[Y + Z] − H[Y].
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
An entropy analogue of Plünnecke's inequality; it generalizes Kaimanovich–Vershik.
proofSteps: By (A.9), I[X : Z|X+Y+Z] = H[X, X+Y+Z] + H[Z, X+Y+Z] − H[X, Z, X+Y+Z] − H[X+Y+Z].
By independence (A.4): H[X, X+Y+Z] = H[X] + H[Y+Z], H[Z, X+Y+Z] = H[Z] + H[X+Y], and H[X, Z, X+Y+Z] = H[X] + H[Y] + H[Z]. The claim becomes I[X : Z|X+Y+Z] ≥ 0 (A.8).
acceptance: Z = 0 gives an equality.

nodes.title: Entropic Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers lemma (Lemma A.2)
nodes.statement: Let (A, B) be a G²-valued random variable and Z = A + B. Then Σ_z p_Z(z) d[(A|Z=z); (B|Z=z)] ≤ 3I[A : B] + 2H[Z] − H[A] − H[B].
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
A, B are jointly distributed, not assumed independent; 2H[Z] − H[A] − H[B] is not 2d[A; B].
proofSteps: Take (A₁, B₁), (A₂, B₂) conditionally independent trials of (A, B) relative to Z; then H[A₁, B₁, A₂, B₂] = 2H[A,B] − H[Z] (A.17), and the left side is H[A₁ − B₂|Z] − ½H[A₁|Z] − ½H[B₂|Z] (A.18).

Submodularity (A.19): H[A₁ − B₂] + H[A₁ − B₂, A₁, B₁] ≤ H[A₁ − B₂, A₁] + H[A₁ − B₂, B₁]. The second term is 2H[A,B] − H[Z]; each term on the right is at most H[A] + H[B], using A₁ − B₂ = A₂ − B₁ (A.20)–(A.22).
So H[A₁ − B₂|Z] ≤ H[A₁ − B₂] ≤ 2I[A : B] + H[Z], and H[A₁|Z] = H[B₂|Z] = H[A] + H[B] − I[A : B] − H[Z].
acceptance: The source improves the constants of Tao's entropic BSG [37, Lemma 3.3].

sources.locator: Appendix A, Lemma A.2 and proof, pp. 30–32 (AAM)
sources.match: The lemma and its proof.

nodes.title: The fibring lemma (Proposition 4.1)
nodes.statement: Let π: H → H′ be a homomorphism of finite abelian groups and Z₁, Z₂ H-valued random variables. Then d[Z₁; Z₂] ≥ d[π(Z₁); π(Z₂)] + d[Z₁|π(Z₁); Z₂|π(Z₂)]. If Z₁, Z₂ are independent, the difference is I[Z₁ − Z₂ : (π(Z₁), π(Z₂)) | π(Z₁ − Z₂)] (4.1).
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
proofSteps: Take Z₁, Z₂ independent. By (A.15), d[Z₁|π(Z₁); Z₂|π(Z₂)] = H[Z₁ − Z₂|π(Z₁), π(Z₂)] − ½H[Z₁|π(Z₁)] − ½H[Z₂|π(Z₂)] ≤ H[Z₁ − Z₂|π(Z₁ − Z₂)] − … by submodularity.
H[Z₁ − Z₂|π(Z₁ − Z₂)] = H[Z₁ − Z₂] − H[π(Z₁ − Z₂)] and H[Zᵢ|π(Zᵢ)] = H[Zᵢ] − H[π(Zᵢ)], so the bound is d[Z₁; Z₂] − d[π(Z₁); π(Z₂)].
The slack is H[A|B] − H[A|B,C] = I[A : C|B] with A = Z₁ − Z₂, B = π(Z₁ − Z₂), C = (π(Z₁), π(Z₂)), and C determines B.
acceptance: π = 0 gives d[Z₁|0; Z₂|0] = d[Z₁; Z₂]; π = id gives d[Z₁; Z₂] ≥ d[Z₁; Z₂] + 0.

sources.match: The proposition, with its explicit error term.

nodes.title: Fibring for four independent variables (Corollary 4.2)
nodes.statement: For independent Y₁, Y₂, Y₃, Y₄ in a finite abelian group, d[Y₁ − Y₃; Y₂ − Y₄] + d[Y₁|Y₁ − Y₃; Y₂|Y₂ − Y₄] + I[Y₁ − Y₂ : Y₂ − Y₄ | Y₁ − Y₂ − Y₃ + Y₄] = d[Y₁; Y₂] + d[Y₃; Y₄].
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
In characteristic 2 every sign may be replaced by + (Remark 4.3).
proofSteps: Apply Proposition 4.1 with H = G × G, H′ = G, π(x, y) = x − y, Z₁ = (Y₁, Y₃), Z₂ = (Y₂, Y₄); by independence d[Z₁; Z₂] = d[Y₁; Y₂] + d[Y₃; Y₄].
Once π(Z₁) = Y₁ − Y₃ is fixed, Z₁ and Y₁ determine each other; so d[Z₁|π(Z₁); Z₂|π(Z₂)] = d[Y₁|Y₁ − Y₃; Y₂|Y₂ − Y₄].
The conditioning variable in (4.1) is π(Z₁ − Z₂) = π(Z₁) − π(Z₂) = Y₁ − Y₂ − Y₃ + Y₄; the source prints π(Z₁) + π(Z₂) (E5). Given it, Y₁ − Y₂ determines Y₃ − Y₄, and Y₂ − Y₄ determines Y₁ − Y₃.

nodes.title: Conditioning costs at most half the mutual information (Lemma 5.2)
nodes.statement: d[X|Z; Y|W] ≤ d[X; Y] + ½I[X : Z] + ½I[Y : W].
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
proofSteps: With independent copies, d[X|Z; Y|W] = H[X′ − Y′|Z′, W′] − ½H[X′|Z′] − ½H[Y′|W′] ≤ H[X′ − Y′] − ½H[X′|Z′] − ½H[Y′|W′] by (A.5), which is d[X′; Y′] + ½I[X′ : Z′] + ½I[Y′ : W′].
acceptance: Z, W constant gives equality.

nodes.title: Distances to sums and to fibres (Lemma 5.3)
nodes.statement: For Y, Z independent: d[X; Y − Z] − d[X; Y] ≤ ½(H[Y − Z] − H[Y]) = ½d[Y; Z] + ¼H[Z] − ¼H[Y] (5.6), and d[X; Y|Y − Z] − d[X; Y] ≤ ½(H[Y − Z] − H[Z]) = ½d[Y; Z] + ¼H[Y] − ¼H[Z] (5.7).
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
proofSteps: (5.6): take X independent of (Y, Z); then d[X; Y − Z] − d[X; Y] = H[X − Y + Z] − H[X − Y] − ½H[Y − Z] + ½H[Y], and Madiman's inequality with Y replaced by −Y bounds the first difference by H[Y − Z] − H[Y].
(5.7): I[Y : Y − Z] = H[Y − Z] − H[Z]; apply Lemma 5.2 to (X, trivial) and (Y, Y − Z).
acceptance: The source thanks Floris van Doorn for a sign correction to this statement found in the Lean formalization (footnote 7).

nodes.title: Distance to a fibre of a double sum (Lemma 7.1)
nodes.statement: For Y, Z, Z′ independent: d[X; Y − Z|Y − Z − Z′] − d[X; Y] ≤ ½(H[Y − Z − Z′] + H[Y − Z] − H[Y] − H[Z′]).
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
proofSteps: (5.7) with Y ↦ Y − Z and Z ↦ Z′ gives d[X; Y − Z|Y − Z − Z′] − d[X; Y − Z] ≤ ½(H[Y − Z − Z′] − H[Z′]); add (5.6).

nodes.title: Distance zero means cosets of one subgroup (Lemma 2.2)
nodes.statement: If d[X₁; X₂] = 0, there is a subgroup H ≤ G such that p_{X₁} and p_{X₂} are translates of U_H; in particular d[X₁; U_H] = d[X₂; U_H] = 0.
hypotheses: All random variables take values in finite types; Ω is a probability space and conditioning on an event of probability zero contributes zero weight.
G is any finite abelian group; the source states it for G = 𝔽₂ⁿ.
proofSteps: For independent copies, H[X₁′ − X₂′] ≥ H[X₁′ − X₂′|X₂′] = H[X₁′] and likewise H[X₂′]; averaging gives d ≥ 0, so equality holds in both, and X₁′ − X₂′ is independent of X₂′ and of X₁′. Hence p_{X₁ − s₂} = p_{X₁ − X₂} = p_{s₁ − X₂} for s₁, s₂ in the supports (2.4).
Let H = Sym(X₁) = Sym(X₂) = Sym(X₁ − X₂), the stabilizer of the distribution under translation; it is a subgroup contained in S − S. From (2.4), S₁ − S₁ = S₂ − S₂ = H.
H[X₁] = H[X₁ + U_H] ≥ log|H| by (A.11), while H[X₁] ≤ log|S₁| ≤ log|S₁ − S₁| = log|H|. Equality throughout forces X₁ uniform on S₁ = a₁ + H; likewise X₂.
acceptance: A Dirac mass is uniform on a coset of the trivial subgroup.

nodes.title: The functional τ and its minimizers
nodes.statement: For η > 0 and fixed reference distributions X₁⁰, X₂⁰ on G = 𝔽₂ⁿ, τ[X₁; X₂] = d[X₁; X₂] + ηd[X₁⁰; X₁] + ηd[X₂⁰; X₂] (2.1). A τ-minimizer is a pair of probability distributions minimizing τ; the source uses η = 1/9.
hypotheses: τ depends only on the distributions of X₁, X₂; the references are never modified.
In Lean, G is a finite ℤ/2-module; the definition makes sense for any finite abelian group.
proofSteps: Define tau and IsTauMinimizer on probability measures.
Existence: the pairs of probability distributions on the finite set G form a compact set, and d is continuous, so τ attains its minimum.
(2.3): τ[X₂⁰; X₁⁰] = (1 + 2η)d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰], by symmetry of d.
The conditioned form (3.15): minimality gives d[X₁′|Y₁; X₂′|Y₂] ≥ k − η(d[X₁⁰; X₁′|Y₁] − d[X₁⁰; X₁]) − η(d[X₂⁰; X₂′|Y₂] − d[X₂⁰; X₂]), by applying (3.12) to each pair of fibres and averaging.
acceptance: The argument is not constructive because of the compactness step; Remark 2.3 sketches an algorithmic variant with worse constants.

nodes.title: First estimate: I₁ ≤ 2ηk (Section 5)
nodes.statement: In the minimizer setting, I₁ = I[X₁ + X₂ : X̃₁ + X₂ | S] ≤ 2ηk (3.13), and H[S] ≤ ½H[X₁] + ½H[X₂] + (2 + η)k − I₁ (5.8).
hypotheses: G is an elementary abelian 2-group (a finite ℤ/2-module, i.e. 𝔽₂ⁿ); η = 1/9; ρ₁, ρ₂ are the reference distributions X₁⁰, X₂⁰; (μ₁, μ₂) minimizes τ; X₁, X₂, X̃₁, X̃₂ are independent with X₁, X̃₁ ∼ μ₁ and X₂, X̃₂ ∼ μ₂; k = d[X₁; X₂] and S = X₁ + X₂ + X̃₁ + X̃₂.
proofSteps: Corollary 4.2 with (Y₁, Y₂, Y₃, Y₄) = (X₁, X₂, X̃₂, X̃₁) gives d[X₁ + X̃₂; X₂ + X̃₁] + d[X₁|X₁ + X̃₂; X₂|X₂ + X̃₁] + I₁ = 2k (5.1).

Minimality (3.12), (3.15) bounds each distance below by k − η(…) (5.2). Lemma 5.3 bounds each bracket: the four differences are ½k ± ¼(H[X₂] − H[X₁]), and they add in pairs to k (5.3), (5.4). So I₁ ≤ 2ηk.
Subtracting (5.2) from (5.1) and using (5.4) gives d[X₁ + X̃₂; X₂ + X̃₁] ≤ (1 + η)k − I₁, which is (5.8) because H[X₁ + X̃₂] = H[X₂ + X̃₁] = k + ½H[X₁] + ½H[X₂].
acceptance: Only I₁ = O(ηk) is needed for some constant in Theorem 1.8 (Remark 5.1).

sources.match: The estimate and the entropy bound (5.8).

nodes.title: Second estimate: the bound (3.14) on I₂ (Section 6)
nodes.statement: In the minimizer setting, I₂ = I[X₁ + X₂ : X₁ + X̃₁ | S] ≤ 2ηk + 2η(2ηk − I₁)/(1 − η).
hypotheses: G is an elementary abelian 2-group (a finite ℤ/2-module, i.e. 𝔽₂ⁿ); η = 1/9; ρ₁, ρ₂ are the reference distributions X₁⁰, X₂⁰; (μ₁, μ₂) minimizes τ; X₁, X₂, X̃₁, X̃₂ are independent with X₁, X̃₁ ∼ μ₁ and X₂, X̃₂ ∼ μ₂; k = d[X₁; X₂] and S = X₁ + X₂ + X̃₁ + X̃₂.
By symmetry I₃ = I[X̃₁ + X₂ : X₁ + X̃₁ | S] equals I₂.
proofSteps: Corollary 4.2 with (X₂, X₁, X̃₂, X̃₁) gives d[X₁ + X̃₁; X₂ + X̃₂] + d[X₁|X₁ + X̃₁; X₂|X₂ + X̃₂] + I₂ = 2k.
Minimality and Lemma 5.3 (each bracket at most ½d[Xᵢ; Xᵢ]) give I₂ ≤ η(d[X₁; X₁] + d[X₂; X₂]) (6.4) and d[X₁ + X̃₁; X₂ + X̃₂] ≥ k − (η/2)(d[X₁; X₁] + d[X₂; X₂]) (6.5).

Expanding the same distance and using (5.8) gives d[X₁ + X̃₁; X₂ + X̃₂] ≤ (2 + η)k − ½(d[X₁; X₁] + d[X₂; X₂]) − I₁; with (6.5), d[X₁; X₁] + d[X₂; X₂] ≤ 2k + 2(2ηk − I₁)/(1 − η) (6.6), and (6.4) concludes.
acceptance: The Ruzsa triangle inequality would give the weaker bound 4ηk.

sources.match: The estimate and its proof.

nodes.title: The endgame construction (Lemma 7.2)
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝔽₂ⁿ and (T₁, T₂, T₃) be G³-valued with T₁ + T₂ + T₃ = 0, and δ = Σ_{i<j} I[Tᵢ : Tⱼ]. Then there are T₁′, T₂′ with d[T₁′; T₂′] + η(d[X₁⁰; T₁′] − d[X₁⁰; X₁]) + η(d[X₂⁰; T₂′] − d[X₂⁰; X₂]) ≤ δ + (η/3)(δ + Σ_{i=1}^{2} Σ_{j=1}^{3} (d[Xᵢ⁰; Tⱼ] − d[Xᵢ⁰; Xᵢ])).
hypotheses: The source writes I[Tᵢ; Tⱼ] in (7.5) for the mutual information I[Tᵢ : Tⱼ] (E6).
η ≥ 0 and the references X₁⁰, X₂⁰ and X₁, X₂ are as in the τ setting.
proofSteps: Entropic BSG with (A, B) = (T₁, T₂) (so A + B = T₃): Σ_t p_{T₃}(t) d[(T₁|T₃=t); (T₂|T₃=t)] ≤ 3I[T₁ : T₂] + 2H[T₃] − H[T₁] − H[T₂] = δ, because each pair of the Tᵢ determines the third.
Lemma 5.2: d[X₁⁰; T₁|T₃] − d[X₁⁰; X₁] ≤ d[X₁⁰; T₁] − d[X₁⁰; X₁] + ½I[T₁ : T₃], and likewise for T₂.
Choose t₃ minimizing ψ[(T₁|T₃=t₃); (T₂|T₃=t₃)] (7.7). Do the same for all six permutations and average: each Tⱼ occurs twice in each position, and the mutual-information terms average to δ/3.
acceptance: If δ = 0 the Tᵢ are pairwise independent and two of them already work, by (3.9).

sources.match: The lemma and its proof; (7.5) notation corrected (E6).

nodes.title: A τ-minimizer has distance zero (Proposition 2.1)
nodes.statement: Let η = 1/9. If (X₁, X₂) minimizes τ, then d[X₁; X₂] = 0. Equivalently (Proposition 2.1), if d[X₁; X₂] > 0 there are X₁′, X₂′ with τ[X₁′; X₂′] < τ[X₁; X₂].
hypotheses: G is an elementary abelian 2-group (a finite ℤ/2-module, i.e. 𝔽₂ⁿ); η = 1/9; ρ₁, ρ₂ are the reference distributions X₁⁰, X₂⁰; (μ₁, μ₂) minimizes τ; X₁, X₂, X̃₁, X̃₂ are independent with X₁, X̃₁ ∼ μ₁ and X₂, X̃₂ ∼ μ₂; k = d[X₁; X₂] and S = X₁ + X₂ + X̃₁ + X̃₂.
proofSteps: Set U = X₁ + X₂, V = X̃₁ + X₂, W = X₁ + X̃₁; then I₁ = I[U : V|S], I₂ = I[W : U|S], I₃ = I[V : W|S], and by the two estimates their sum is at most 6ηk − ((1 − 5η)/(1 − η))(2ηk − I₁) (7.2).
Six applications of Lemma 7.1 and (5.8) give Σ_{i,A∈{U,V,W}} (d[Xᵢ⁰; A|S] − d[Xᵢ⁰; Xᵢ]) ≤ (6 − 3η)k + 3(2ηk − I₁) (7.3); for W the distance to X₂⁰ is computed through W′ = X₂ + X̃₂ = W + S.
Characteristic 2: U + V + W = 0 (7.4). Apply Lemma 7.2 to (U, V, W | S = s), then minimality (3.12), and average over s: k ≤ δ̃ + (η/3)(δ̃ + Σ(…)) (7.8).
Combine: k ≤ (8η + η²)k − c(2ηk − I₁) with c ≥ 0 when η(2η + 17) ≤ 3, and 2ηk − I₁ ≥ 0 by (3.13). For η = 1/9, 8η + η² = 73/81 < 1, so k = 0.
acceptance: Over ℤ the statement fails: discrete Gaussians are near-minimal (p. 14); the characteristic-2 identity (7.4) is essential.

sources.match: The proposition and the endgame computation.

nodes.title: Entropic polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa theorem (Theorem 1.8)
nodes.statement: Let G = 𝔽₂ⁿ and X₁⁰, X₂⁰ G-valued random variables. There is a subgroup H ≤ G with d[X₁⁰; U_H] + d[X₂⁰; U_H] ≤ 11d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰]; moreover each of d[X₁⁰; U_H], d[X₂⁰; U_H] is at most 6d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰].
hypotheses: U_H is the uniform distribution on H. In Lean, G is a finite ℤ/2-module.
proofSteps: Take a τ-minimizer (X₁, X₂) (compactness). By Proposition 2.1, d[X₁; X₂] = 0, so Lemma 2.2 gives H with d[X₁; U_H] = d[X₂; U_H] = 0.
The triangle inequality gives d[Xᵢ⁰; U_H] = d[Xᵢ⁰; Xᵢ], so η(d[X₁⁰; U_H] + d[X₂⁰; U_H]) = τ[X₁; X₂] ≤ τ[X₂⁰; X₁⁰] = (1 + 2η)d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰] (2.3). With η = 1/9 this is 11d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰].
|d[X₁⁰; U_H] − d[X₂⁰; U_H]| ≤ d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰] by the triangle inequality, so each is at most 6d[X₁⁰; X₂⁰].
acceptance: X₁⁰ = X₂⁰ uniform on a subgroup H gives H itself, with all distances 0.

nodes.title: Marton's conjecture in characteristic 2 (Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: If A ⊆ 𝔽₂ⁿ is nonempty with |A + A| ≤ K|A|, then A is covered by at most 2K¹² cosets of some subgroup H ≤ 𝔽₂ⁿ of size at most |A|.
hypotheses: C = 12 comes from C′ = 11 in Theorem 1.8. Liao's refinement (C = 11, then 9) is not planned.
proofSteps: With U_A uniform on A, H[U_A] = log|A| and H[U_A + U_A′] ≤ log|A + A|, so d[U_A; U_A] ≤ log K. Theorem 1.8 gives H with d[U_A; U_H] ≤ ½C′ log K (B.1), hence |log|H| − log|A|| ≤ C′ log K (B.2).
(B.1) says H[U_A − U_H] ≤ ½log(|A||H|) + ½C′ log K; by (A.2) some x₀ has |A ∩ (H + x₀)| ≥ K^{−C′/2}|A|^{1/2}|H|^{1/2}.
Ruzsa covering (Mathlib ruzsa_covering_mul, additive form) covers A by at most K|A|/|A ∩ (H + x₀)| ≤ K^{C′/2+1}(|A|/|H|)^{1/2} translates of (A ∩ (H + x₀)) − (A ∩ (H + x₀)) ⊆ H.
If |H| ≤ |A| this is at most K^{C′+1} by (B.2). Otherwise cover H by at most 2|H|/|A| cosets of a subgroup H′ with |H′| ≤ |A|, giving at most 2K^{C′/2+1}(|H|/|A|)^{1/2} ≤ 2K^{C′+1} cosets.
acceptance: If A is a subgroup, K = 1 and one coset suffices.
Conversely, a cover by r cosets of H with |H| ≤ |A| gives |A + A| ≤ (r(r−1)/2 + 1)|A|, so the theorem is polynomially sharp (p. 1).
The factor 2 is needed when A is most of a subgroup (footnote 1).

sources.locator: §1, Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2; Appendix B, pp. 32–33 (AAM)

nodes.title: Spectral Bogolyubov theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a nonempty subset of a finite abelian group G, ρ=|A|/|G|, K>0 and |A+A|≤K|A|, then Λ=Spec_(ρ/(2√K))(1_A) has |Λ|≤4K/ρ and B_ch(Λ,1/4)⊆2A−2A. The inverse Fourier sum of |1̂_A|⁴ has real part at least (5/16)Σχ|1̂_A(χ)|⁴ on this Bohr set.

proofSteps: Energy Cauchy–Schwarz gives fourth mass at least ρ³/K. The complementary mass is at most ρ³/(4K), so the selected mass is at least three quarters of the total.
Each resonant character has real part greater than 3/4. Subtracting the tail leaves (3/4)(3/4)−1/4=5/16 times total mass, correcting E1.
Fourier inversion of the fourfold convolution gives |G|^−3 times the number of representations x=a₁+a₂−a₃−a₄. Positive mass therefore proves the containment.

nodes.title: Generalized arithmetic progression

nodes.title: Filtered polynomial sequence
nodes.statement: For a degree filtration G_• and g:ℤ^ℓ→G, put ∂_h g(n)=g(n+h)g(n)^−1. The sequence is polynomial when every r-fold iterated derivative belongs to G_r, for every choice of directions and base point; the zero-fold condition is g(n)∈G₀.
hypotheses: ℓ≥1 for the analytic endpoints; the algebraic definition also makes sense at ℓ=0. Iterated derivative order is fixed, since the target can be noncommutative.
proofSteps: Iterate the concrete multiplicative derivative through a list of integer vectors. Bundle the membership condition. The general polynomial-map group theorem and Taylor expansion are distinct key inputs.
acceptance: On additive ℝ with degree-one filtration, g(n)=a+bn is polynomial.
g(n)=n² on additive ℝ is not polynomial for the degree-one filtration, since its second derivative is 2.
The same sequence is polynomial for the degree-two filtration with G₂=ℝ and G₃=0.
For g(n)=a^n b, ∂_h g(n)=a^h; reversing the product convention can introduce conjugation.

nodes.title: Filtered nilmanifold
nodes.statement: A degree-s filtered nilmanifold consists of a finite-dimensional real connected simply connected nilpotent Lie group G, a degree-s filtration by closed connected Lie subgroups G_i, and a discrete subgroup Γ with compact right-coset space G/Γ. For every i, Γ∩G_i is cocompact in G_i. Γ need not be normal.
hypotheses: The quotient is a homogeneous space, not generally a quotient group. Use the native smooth Lie-group structure and native subgroup/coset topology.
proofSteps: Bundle the native Lie-group and simply-connected-space instances, the filtration and lattice. Import the global nilpotent exponential, smooth homogeneous quotient and invariant probability measure from LieGroups, Part II.
acceptance: ℝ/ℤ with the degree-one filtration is the circle.
The real Heisenberg group modulo its integer lattice is compact, but the lattice is not normal.
ℝ/ℚ fails the discrete-lattice requirement.
ℝ/{0} fails compactness.

nodes.title: Rational adapted Mal’cev coordinates
nodes.statement: For a filtered nilmanifold of dimension m, a Q-rational adapted Mal’cev basis X₁,…,X_m of log G has bracket coefficients c_ijk∈ℚ of reduced height max(|numerator|,denominator)≤Q, global second-kind coordinates g=exp(t₁X₁)⋯exp(t_mX_m), and Γ corresponding exactly to ℤ^m. Each log G_i is the span of the final dim G_i basis vectors. Complexity≤M means Q≤M for such an adapted basis; dimension is a separate parameter.
hypotheses: Q,M≥1. First-kind exponential coordinates and second-kind ordered coordinates are distinct. The exponential is the Lie-group exponential.
proofSteps: Use the native Lie algebra of left-invariant derivations. Import its identification with the tangent Lie algebra and global exponential from LieGroups, Part II. Store the basis, rational bracket data and adapted global coordinate equivalence.
acceptance: For additive ℝ^m and standard basis, brackets vanish and both coordinate systems are the identity.
The reduced height of 2/3 is 3, and irrational √2 has no finite rational height.
In the Heisenberg group, ordered exponential coordinates differ from first-kind coordinates by the central cross term.
On ℝ/ℤ, a basis vector 2 does not identify the lattice with integer second-kind coordinates.

nodes.title: Mal’cev metric and bounded nilsequence
nodes.statement: For second-kind coordinates ψ, define d_G(x,y) as the infimum of finite-chain sums with edge cost min(‖ψ(uv^−1)‖∞,‖ψ(vu^−1)‖∞). Define d_(G/Γ)(xΓ,yΓ)=inf_(γ,γ′∈Γ)d_G(xγ,yγ′). For F:G/Γ→ℂ put ‖F‖Lip=‖F‖∞+Lip(F). A bounded degree-s nilsequence is n↦F(g(n)Γ), with g filtered polynomial and |F|≤1; its dimension, basis height and Lipschitz bound are separate data.
hypotheses: The group metric is right invariant. The minimum in the edge cost and the infimum over both representatives follow the source exactly.
proofSteps: Construct the chain metric, prove it induces the manifold topology, and descend it through the right-lattice isometry action.
Use the imported compact homogeneous probability measure. Bundle g,F and a nonnegative Lipschitz constant L with |F(x)−F(y)|≤L d(x,y); the source Lipschitz norm is bounded by 1+L.

Circle representatives x and x+3 give the same quotient distance.
g(n)=αn on ℝ and F(x)=exp(2πix) give a degree-one phase.

nodes.title: Horizontal character, smoothness and equidistribution
nodes.statement: A horizontal character is a continuous homomorphism η:G→ℝ with η(Γ)⊆ℤ, viewed modulo ℤ. Its integer coefficient vector in Mal’cev coordinates defines its size. For a binomial polynomial P(n)=Σ_(j=0)^s α_j binom(n,j), put ‖P‖C∞[N]=max_(1≤j≤s)N^j dist(α_j,ℤ). A finite orbit is δ-equidistributed if its average differs from invariant probability integration by at most δ‖F‖Lip for every Lipschitz F; it is totally δ-equidistributed if the same holds on every subprogression of length at least δN.
hypotheses: N≥1, 0<δ<1; the constant coefficient is excluded from C∞. Kai’s starred monomial norm is a different norm and is related by bounded-degree integer-denominator conversion.
proofSteps: Use the native continuous homomorphism type and integer lattice-annihilation condition. Define the finite averages and invariant integrals with the metric fixed above.
acceptance: P(n)=√2 has smoothness zero.
P(n)=n/4 has smoothness N/4.
P(n)=binom(n,2)/2 has smoothness N²/2, whereas its monomial quadratic coefficient is 1/4.
A constant orbit on the circle is not δ-equidistributed for all δ>0.
On ℝ/ℤ, lifted horizontal characters are x↦mx for m∈ℤ.

nodes.title: Finite nilsequence factor and regular resolution
nodes.statement: For bounded real functions h₁,…,h_T on [N] and K>0, partition [N] by the finite label vector (floor(Kh_i(n)))_i. Its conditional average of f on a cell is the cell mean. A resolution K for h is C-regular when, for every r>0, the proportion of n with dist(Kh(n),ℤ)≤r is at most 2Cr. Joins refine all the chosen labels.
hypotheses: Use a native finite partition. Empty cells are omitted; no infinite measure-theoretic conditional expectation is redefined here.

acceptance: A constant label gives one cell, and its conditional average is the global mean.
Joining a partition with itself preserves its cells.

Put Λ_(χ,R)(n)=(log R)Σ_(d|n)μ(d)χ(log d/log R), W=∏_(p≤w)p, b∈{1,…,W} coprime to W, and R=N^(1/(k2^(k+3))). On the representative half-window N/2≤n<N define ν(n)=(φ(W)/W)Λ_(χ,R)(Wn+b)²/(c_χlog R); outside it set ν=1. The modified prime weight is (φ(W)/W)log(Wn+b) on shifted primes and zero elsewhere.
hypotheses: N prime and sufficiently large; w tends to infinity sufficiently slowly. Divisors of a nonzero integer mean positive divisors of its absolute value. The selected cutoff is fixed throughout the proof.
proofSteps: Use native Möbius, totient, positive divisors and primality. The smooth truncated divisor sum is the SV.1-owned sieve-weight variant requested below.

At a shifted prime larger than R only the divisor one contributes, so Λ_(χ,R)=log R. This gives domination by a fixed positive multiple δ_k=1/(c_χk2^(k+4)) of the modified prime weight on the half-window for sufficiently large N.
acceptance: w=1 gives W=1 and w=5 gives W=30.
A representative n<N/2 receives weight one.
At p>R the only nonzero divisor contribution is d=1, so the weight is log R.
For W=6,b=1,n=1 the shifted integer 7 is prime, although n is not prime.
For W=6,b=1,n=4 the shifted integer 25 gives zero.

nodes.title: Smooth divisor linear-forms moments
nodes.statement: Fix m,t,L and nonzero integer affine forms ψ₁,…,ψ_m:ℤ^t→ℤ with pairwise nonproportional rational slopes and bounded coefficients L. For W as above, b coprime to W, R→∞ with R=o(N^(1/(10m))), and a product box whose side lengths are at least R^(10m), E_x∏_(i=1)^mΛ_(χ,R)(Wψ_i(x)+b)²=(1+o_(m,t,L,χ)(1))(Wc_χlog R/φ(W))^m.
hypotheses: w→∞ sufficiently slowly. The average is over the integer box and is uniform in permitted b and offsets of size O_L(N). Nonzero shifted arguments are required when defining divisor sums.
proofSteps: Expand the divisor sums and impose divisibility with the Chinese remainder theorem; control boundary counts using the side-length hypothesis.

Use smooth Fourier inversion with rapid decay to form the Euler product. At p≤w coprimality removes all local divisibilities; at large p use pairwise slope independence to bound multiple intersections by O(p^−2).

Factor the product into zeta functions near one approached from the right half-plane. The built-in pole asymptotic and smooth Fourier decay control the remainder; no classical zero-free region is required.

nodes.title: Arbitrarily long prime progressions
nodes.statement: For every k≥1 and lower bound H, there are a>H and r≥1 such that a,a+r,…,a+(k−1)r are all prime.
hypotheses: The selected proof uses the smooth linear-forms-only majorant. It also yields a relative-density extension when the weighted-density bridge is supplied.
proofSteps: For each fixed w, set W to the corresponding primorial and use the fixed-progression prime number theorem at residue 1 modulo W. Subtract its values at WN+1 and WN/2+1 to give modified prime-weight mean tending to 1/2 on the half-window. Choose w(N) tending to infinity sufficiently slowly by diagonalizing both this convergence and the finitely many smooth-majorant moment estimates. This uses no estimate uniform over arbitrary growing moduli.
Scale the shifted prime weight by the fixed domination constant and apply linear-forms-only relative Szemerédi. The r=0 contribution is O_k(log^kN/N), so a nonzero cyclic difference survives.

Every selected point lies in one interval of length less than N/2. Consecutive differences therefore have a unique lift of absolute value less than N/2 and are equal as integers. Reverse the progression if the lifted difference is negative, and undo the W-trick. Let N exceed the prescribed lower bound.

nodes.title: Smooth and rational orbit factors
nodes.statement: A group element γ is M-rational relative to Γ when γ^r∈Γ for some integer 1≤r≤M. A sequence is M-rational when every value has this property; its coset sequence being periodic of period at most M is a separate condition. A sequence ε is (M,N)-smooth when d_G(ε(n),1)≤M and d_G(ε(n),ε(n−1))≤M/N for all n∈[N]. A connected subgroup H is M-rational when its Lie algebra has a basis of rational combinations of the fixed Mal’cev basis with coefficients of reduced height at most M.
hypotheses: M,N≥1. Pointwise rationality does not by itself supply periodicity of an arbitrary sequence. Smoothness is measured in the right-invariant group metric.
proofSteps: Use actual powers, lattice membership, Lie-algebra spans and the fixed coordinate metric. Record the smooth and rational predicates separately.
acceptance: For additive ℝ/ℤ, 1/3 is 3-rational but not 2-rational.
The identity sequence has zero distance and zero increments.
An arbitrary nonperiodic zero-one choice between circle points 0 and 1/2 is pointwise 2-rational but need not be periodic.

nodes.title: Affine-linear system and Cauchy–Schwarz complexity
nodes.statement: An integer affine system Ψ of t forms in d variables has ψ_i(x)=b_i+v_i·x, with b_i∈ℤ and v_i∈ℤ^d. Its size at scale N is max_i(max(‖v_i‖∞,|b_i|/N)). Its Cauchy–Schwarz complexity is at most s when, for every i, the other indices partition into at most s+1 classes so that v_i is outside the ℚ-linear span of the slopes in each class. This is the affine-span convention allowing constants. Finite complexity excludes proportional slopes.
hypotheses: N≥1, every slope is nonzero for the prime-pattern theorems. Empty classes are allowed; a nonzero slope is outside their zero span.
proofSteps: Use native integer vectors and affine maps, and native rational submodule spans after scalar extension. Encode the finite class assignment for each omitted index.
acceptance: The system x,y has complexity zero.
x,x+r,x+2r has complexity one and not zero.
x,x+2 has infinite complexity.
x,H−x has proportional slopes and infinite complexity.

nodes.statement: For a real primitive Hecke character χ of conductor q and fixed s≥1, its residue-class function on O_K/q satisfies U^(s+1)(χ)≤C_(K,s,ε)N(q)^(−1/2^(s+2)+ε) for every ε>0. The associated Siegel and Cramér models are Gowers-close at the polylogarithmic rates needed for arbitrary fixed log-power error.
hypotheses: The conductor is an ideal. Reduction at odd primes involves polynomials that are not squares over the algebraic closure; a coprime-degree special case of Weil is insufficient. Dyadic factors require a separate conductor bound.
proofSteps: Use ideal Chinese remainder decomposition. For odd residue characteristics, expand the Gowers cube and apply the general multiplicative-character Weil bound to the resulting nonsquare polynomial.
Bound exceptional degeneracies and the dyadic local factors using the primitive quadratic-conductor input.
Combine the conductor decay with the Hecke Siegel-zero model from AN.4 to compare it with the Cramér model.

For every A>1, replacing the Siegel model by the Cramér model gives O_(s,K,A)((log N)^−A).
hypotheses: The arithmetic models and norm-length bases are owned by AN.4. The basis compatibility is required for constants uniform in a. The integer box norm is normalized.

nodes.title: Number-field and localized local factors
nodes.statement: For degree-n K, fractional ideal a and affine ψ_i:ℤ^d→a, define β_p=(p^n/φ_K(p))^t times the proportion of x∈(ℤ/p)^d for which every ψ_i(x) is nonzero in a/𝔭a for every prime ideal 𝔭 above p. The localized factor β_(p,S) imposes this avoidance only for 𝔭∉S, retaining the same multiplier (p^n/φ_K(p))^t. Let C_(S,Ψ)=∏_pβ_(p,S). All conditions above a rational prime use one common x.
hypotheses: φ_K(p)=|(O_K/pO_K)×|. For localized maps choose a finitely generated fractional ideal containing their images, as in Kai Appendix E; the coefficient is independent of that auxiliary choice.
proofSteps: Use native prime ideals and residue quotients, with one finite average over the rational-prime source.

For all but finitely many p, use the full-rank kernel restriction to estimate simultaneous vanishings. Treat removed prime ideals at S separately; they can change the multiplier without leaving an avoidance condition.
acceptance: At K=ℚ and ψ(x)=x the factor is one.
At K=ℚ,t=1 and S={p}, the p-factor is p/(p−1), rather than one.
Separate witnesses for different prime ideals above p do not establish positivity without a common source residue vector.
Removing no prime ideals preserves every factor.

nodes.title: Prime patterns in a localized number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of nonzero prime ideals, a a nonzero fractional ideal and affine ψ_i:ℤ^d→a[S^−1], t,d≥1. Assume each linear part and its restriction to the kernel of every other linear part has torsion cokernel. For A>1, N sufficiently large depending on K,S,Ψ,A, and Ω⊆[−N,N]^d whose boundary is covered by Z Lipschitz maps with constants at most L₀N, Σ_(x∈Ω∩ℤ^d)∏_iΛ_(O_K[S^−1])^a(ψ_i(x))=C_(S,Ψ)vol(Ω)/(res_(s=1)ζ_K(s))^t+O_(K,S,Ψ,Z,L₀,A)(N^d(log N)^−A). The convergent C_(S,Ψ) is positive under the simultaneous local avoidance condition.
hypotheses: The torsion-cokernel condition refers to additive-group quotients and includes individual maps. Ω is measurable and its boundary cover is by maps from [0,1]^(d−1); convex Ω is included. The fixed localized system is not required to have finite cokernel over ℤ.
proofSteps: Choose a finitely generated fractional ideal containing the affine images and spanning the same localized module. Apply localized prime-model uniformity.
Use the vector-valued generalized von Neumann argument and its Lipschitz-boundary extension to replace the weights by localized Cramér models.
Evaluate their product with the ideal sieve in the localized Dedekind ring, using the retained rational-prime multiplier and only the prime ideals outside S.

prototypeLimitations.detail: The prototype bundles native LieGroup, LeftInvariantDerivation, subgroup/coset and topology data. It omits the smooth structures on each layer, the canonical global exponential-product equality, and the Lie-ideal tail condition until the LieGroups supplier gives those interfaces. The first_second_kind API only records the origin compatibility; its full finite triangular BCH comparison is in the reader and the nilsequence-calculus gap. The reader defines the target objects in full; the prototype is not a substitute definition.

The coordinate chain metric and quotient infimum are typed; the API named malcevMetric_comparison gives only a conditional metric comparison implication. Its basis-induced Riemannian construction and uniform constants are stated in the reader and remain supplier/proof gaps.

The vertical obstruction signature gives the weaker r≤dimension bound, while the reader also bounds rank by the abelianization dimension and states the step-lowering quotient. Orbit factorization has a native subgroup embedding and an adapted basis, but omits the bounded rational Lie-algebra change-of-basis condition. These missing conditions are left out explicitly, without proposition stand-ins.

Native ideals, quotient rings, fractional ideals, integer lattice equivalences, prime-weight and Cramér formulae are present as AN.4 consumer sketches. The residue is designated supplier data, not an implemented zeta residue. The Hecke ray-character identification and Siegel-model comparison are omitted. Uniformity is prototyped at its Cramér endpoint with a fixed basis; constants may depend on that basis. The reader also states the exponential Siegel rate, uniform congruence classes and norm-length compatibility.

Finite residue maps test the common-witness and retained-multiplier rules, and native ideal local factors are additionally sketched. Identifying the generic maps with fractional-ideal residue fields, and the product formula under O_K-linearity, remains arithmetic supplier work. The localized module, weights and singular constant are named data interfaces with proof-placeholder bodies, not completed arithmetic definitions. No opaque proposition stands for these missing identifications.

The majorantNu_isKPseudorandom signature assembles an already supplied measure, linear-forms condition and correlation condition. It does not establish these analytic hypotheses for the sharp weight.
